Dowladda Federaalka Galmudug Hiiraan News Jubaland News Koonfur Galbeed SSC Somaliland Follow us Search News Somalia UN political mission in Somalia closes after decades of support Posted by: Horseed Staff The United Nations is ending its political mission in Somalia, bringing to a close a chapter of international engagement that has accompanied the country through decades of conflict, political change and efforts to rebuild state institutions. 31 October, 2026 Share Tweet UN Somalia/Adihamiid Mohamed Raisedon Zenenga, Officer-in-Charge of UNTMIS, delivers remarks at a ceremony marking the closure of the mission. The UN Transitional Assistance Mission in Somalia (UNTMIS) formally wraps up its work on Saturday, with the organisation saying responsibility for the country’s recovery will increasingly rest with Somali institutions. UN Deputy Special Representative James Swan said the mission’s closure came after “considerable progress” in Somalia, while acknowledging that significant challenges remained. “Somalia today possesses national and federal institutions that did not exist when the UN’s political engagement began,” said UN Deputy Special Representative Adam Abdelmoula Zenenga. He pointed to progress in state formation, political inclusion, constitutional processes, human rights frameworks and the development of governance structures that allow for Somali-led decision-making. However, Mr Zenenga said continued international engagement would remain important to sustaining those gains and addressing unresolved priorities. From civil war to state-building Somalia has undergone profound change since the early 1990s, when the collapse of central government institutions and the outbreak of civil war plunged the country into prolonged conflict and instability. The crisis triggered a major movement of refugees and internally displaced people. Insecurity, disputed electoral processes and constitutional reform efforts have added to the difficulties, while repeated droughts and floods have compounded humanitarian needs. Successive UN political missions have supported Somalia through key stages of its peacebuilding and state-building efforts, including attempts to restore governance, rebuild institutions and promote national reconciliation. With UNTMIS now closing, those responsibilities will increasingly be carried by Somali institutions, alongside continued support from UN agencies operating in the country. UN agencies continue humanitarian work The closure of UNTMIS does not mark the end of the UN’s presence in Somalia. About 25 UN entities continue to operate across the country, providing humanitarian and development assistance. In September, the UN migration agency, IOM, helped rehabilitate a vegetable market in the town of Balcad. The renovated market has 56 stalls, running water and solar lighting, with about 70% of the stalls allocated to women-headed households, women-led businesses and small enterprises. Somalia’s health ministry, working with Unicef, has also introduced national guidelines for the care of newborn babies, including those who are premature, small or sick. In Puntland, the UN food agency FAO is supporting a school meals programme connecting 1,330 local farmers and fisherfolk with schools serving about 18,700 children. Meanwhile, in Baidoa, UN mine-action specialists have worked with Somali authorities to teach hundreds of students and teachers how to identify the dangers posed by explosive remnants of war. Humanitarian needs remain severe Despite progress in state-building, Somalia continues to face a complex humanitarian crisis. The UN’s humanitarian affairs office, OCHA, says conflict and climate-related shocks continue to reinforce each other. Families displaced by drought or violence can face further displacement as a result of flooding or renewed fighting. An estimated 4.8 million people in Somalia — out of a population of just under 20 million — require humanitarian assistance this year. Aid organisations have appealed for $852m to provide assistance to 2.4 million people. By mid-October, about 35% of the requested funding had been received. The UN has also called for continued international support to counter the threat posed by the militant group al-Shabab and to help Somalia move towards a gradual and sustainable security transition. Poverty and economic pressures For Somalia’s leaders, tackling poverty is likely to remain a major challenge as the country moves beyond the UN political mission. The economy remains fragile and heavily dependent on subsistence farming, livestock, pastoralism and money sent home by Somalis living abroad. The country also relies heavily on imports, with more than 90% of essential goods coming from overseas, according to OCHA. The combination of poverty, insecurity, climate shocks and limited economic opportunities presents a continuing challenge to the country’s long-term recovery. ‘A new chapter’ The closure of UNTMIS marks a change in the nature of the UN’s engagement with Somalia rather than a complete withdrawal. Humanitarian and development agencies will continue to operate in the country, supporting government institutions and communities. “Today is not an end to the partnership between the United Nations and Somalia,” Mr Zenenga said. “It marks the conclusion of one chapter and the beginning of another.” Explore more on these topics Mogadishu Somalia UN Related Posts Somalia says it will not take sides in Ethiopia-Eritrea tensions 1 min read Egypt and Somalia discuss ties and regional security at Russia-Africa summit 1 min read Ethiopia reportedly plans to withdraw more than 3,000 troops from Somalia 2 min read UN mission closes in Somalia after three decades as political tensions persist 4 min read Back to top Horseed Media About Profile Contact us Privacy Policy Terms and Conditions Category Wararka Soomaaliya Puntland News News Somalia Dowladda Federaalka World News ©2026 Horseed Media Ltd

The United Nations mission in Somalia officially ended its operations on October 31, concluding more than three decades of supporting the Somali government in promoting a democratic transition and building a rule of law state. VietnamPlus • 31/10/2026 Follow Vietnam.vn on G o o g l e Add Vietnam.vn on G o o g l e 0 The United Nations Transitional Assistance Mission in Somalia (UNTMIS) officially concluded its two-year transition period on October 31, bringing to a close more than three decades of peacebuilding operations in the African nation. The United Nations Political Office in Somalia (UNSOM) was established by the UN Security Council in 2013 to support the Somali government in promoting a democratic transition and building a rule of law state, following more than two decades of conflict involving militias, extremist Islamic organizations, and criminal gangs. You may also like In May 2024, Somali President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud proposed that the United Nations terminate the mission before its scheduled end in October of the same year. He later revised the proposal, suggesting a two-year transitional period. During this time, UNSOM was renamed the United Nations Transitional Assistance Mission in Somalia (UNTMIS). In a statement on October 31, Raisedon Zenenga, Acting Head of UNTMIS and Deputy Special Representative of the UN Secretary-General in Somalia, emphasized that the end of the mission's operations does not mean the end of cooperation between the United Nations and Somalia, but rather marks the closing of one phase and the beginning of a new one. According to the plan, the mission's tasks will be handed over to Somali agencies or the group of United Nations agencies operating in the country. The decision to end UNTMIS operations was made amidst a continuing and complex security situation in Somalia. You may also like Al-Shabaab forces – an organization linked to the Al-Qaeda terrorist network and fighting the Somali government for about two decades – continue to control large areas in the central part of the country, despite a large-scale military campaign by Mogadishu with the support of international partners. Ali Mohamed Mohamud Cagabarur Saturday October 31, 2026 Lessons from 1990, the Responsibility of Today’s Intellectuals, and the Dangers of Silence at Critical Moments in a Nation’s History History is not merely a record of events that nations have experienced. It also carries lessons and warnings from which every generation must learn. A nation that fails to learn from the mistakes of its past risks confronting the same tragedies again. Somalia is a clear example of a country where the collapse of state institutions left political, social, and economic wounds from which the nation has yet to fully recover. The collapse of the central government in 1991 was not simply the end of a political system. It triggered institutional breakdown, civil war, mass displacement, and national fragmentation, the consequences of which have affected generations. Today, after decades of efforts to rebuild state institutions, Somalia is once again experiencing political disputes, constitutional disagreements, and growing mistrust among political stakeholders. Although the circumstances today differ significantly from those of 1990, history reminds us of the importance of resolving political differences before they escalate into a national crisis. This raises a question that deserves serious reflection: Where are the Somali intellectuals and respected national figures who will stand up to defend statehood, speak truth to those in power, unite the people, and prevent threats that could undermine the nation’s future? The Lesson of 1990: When Intellectuals Warned of National Collapse In late 1990, as Somalia moved closer to political and security turmoil, a group of prominent Somali intellectuals and respected national figures emerged. They included former politicians, academics, religious scholars, traditional elders, and individuals who commanded considerable respect within society. This group, widely known as the Manifesto Group, sought to play a role in preventing the impending collapse of the Somali state. They called for political reform, dialogue, and a peaceful resolution to the escalating national crisis. The historical significance of their initiative was not limited to the statement they issued. More importantly, it reflected their conviction that intellectual leadership was not merely a matter of titles, prestige, or social recognition. Rather, it carried a patriotic responsibility to speak out when the future of the nation was at risk. Although their efforts ultimately failed to prevent the collapse of the central government in 1991, they left an important historical lesson: individuals possessing knowledge, experience, and social influence have a responsibility to warn of impending dangers, facilitate dialogue, and seek solutions during periods of national crisis. The collapse of 1991 demonstrated that once public confidence, state institutions, and political leadership have been severely undermined, rebuilding them can take decades. The question facing Somalia today is therefore not merely why the state collapsed in 1991, but what lessons we have learned from that experience and what measures we are taking to prevent the repetition of past mistakes. Somalia Today: Political Disputes and the Responsibility of Intellectuals Somalia today is not Somalia of 1990. The country has government institutions, a federal political system, a constitution, and ongoing efforts to strengthen statehood. Nevertheless, the existence of these institutions alone does not guarantee political stability without public trust, accountability, and a shared national understanding of the country's future direction. Constitutional disputes, disagreements between the Federal Government and certain Federal Member States, and differing positions on the electoral process demonstrate the need for inclusive political dialogue. Statehood is not sustained by institutional authority alone. It depends on legitimacy, public confidence, respect for the constitution, and the ability of political leaders to manage disagreements while safeguarding the national interest. When political disagreements are treated as battles in which one side must defeat the other, rather than as issues requiring dialogue and compromise, achieving sustainable solutions becomes increasingly difficult. This is precisely where the responsibility of Somali intellectuals begins. Every society has individuals who may not hold public office but possess knowledge, experience, credibility, and the ability to influence public opinion and political decision-making. Such individuals can serve as bridges between opposing parties, independent voices willing to speak the truth, and constructive forces working to protect the national interest. However, they cannot fulfill this responsibility if they become absorbed in political rivalries, align themselves with competing factions, or remain silent on matters of national importance to protect personal relationships and private interests. True intellectual leadership does not mean agreeing with everything those in power do. It means having the courage to tell them the truth, even when that truth is uncomfortable or unwelcome. The Silence of Intellectuals: A Responsibility That Cannot Be Evaded There is a fundamental difference between neutrality and silence. Neutrality means remaining independent of competing political interests and assessing events according to fairness, evidence, and conscience. Silence, however, when motivated by fear, personal interests, or a desire to please those in power, can amount to an abandonment of one's responsibility to society. Somali intellectuals must be able to engage equally with government leaders, opposition figures, and all political stakeholders. They must speak openly about political mistakes without directing criticism exclusively at one side or defending those with whom they share personal or political interests. Religious scholars, academics, former political leaders, diplomats, businesspeople, traditional elders, women, and young Somalis all share a responsibility to protect social cohesion and the continuity of Somali statehood. Former political leaders and experienced diplomats, in particular, should draw upon the lessons they have learned from leadership, political negotiations, and conflict resolution. Their experience should serve the national interest rather than being confined to commentary and observation. Somalia does not need intellectuals who automatically align themselves with those currently in power or those seeking to replace them. It needs independent national voices whose commitment to the country transcends temporary political interests. A nation cannot be saved through applause and unquestioning praise. It is safeguarded through sincere advice, truthfulness, national unity, and leadership that accepts accountability. The Urgent Need for a National Gathering One of the most important lessons from the efforts of Somali intellectuals in 1990 is that political disputes should not be allowed to deteriorate to the point where peaceful resolution becomes increasingly difficult. Somali intellectuals should initiate independent national consultations to address the country's political situation, constitutional disagreements, electoral processes, and the restoration of confidence in national institutions. Such consultations should remain independent of the Federal Government, Federal Member States, and opposition groups. They should bring together respected individuals known for their integrity, knowledge, impartiality, and experience. The objective should not be to establish another political organization or create a competing center of authority. Rather, it should be to develop a unified civic voice, formulate practical recommendations, and facilitate mediation among political stakeholders. Intellectuals should encourage all parties to resolve constitutional disputes through lawful procedures and dialogue, pursue an electoral process grounded in broad political agreement, and ensure that public authority is exercised in the national interest. Equally important is the need to warn against the exploitation of clan divisions, public incitement, and inflammatory political rhetoric that could intensify tensions. A country that has endured decades of civil conflict and fragmentation needs political leadership willing to compromise and a society capable of preventing political disagreements from escalating into violence. Government and Opposition: A Shared National Responsibility The responsibility to protect Somali statehood does not rest exclusively with those currently in office, nor does it belong solely to the opposition. It is a shared obligation among political stakeholders and society as a whole. Every government has a duty to uphold the constitution, strengthen national institutions, protect citizens' rights, and resolve political disagreements through dialogue and mutual understanding. Similarly, the opposition has a responsibility to present constructive political alternatives, preserve peace, and avoid actions that could undermine the continuity of state institutions. Political disagreement is a natural and legitimate feature of democracy. What matters is ensuring that such disagreements do not destroy the institutions and constitutional principles within which all political actors must operate. Those who hold public office today must recognize that political authority is temporary, while statehood is a national inheritance belonging to both present and future generations. The Somali state must always be greater than the individual who leads it, the political party that governs it, or any group seeking to control it. Conclusion: Let Us Not Become Silent Spectators Whom History Will Hold Accountable Somalia has paid an extraordinarily high price for the collapse of its state institutions. Thousands of families lost loved ones, while millions of Somalis experienced displacement, exile, and hardship as a result of civil conflict and institutional breakdown. Generations of Somalis have grown up without adequate public services, reliable security, or sufficient economic opportunities to build their futures. Today, our generation carries a historic responsibility to protect what has been rebuilt and prevent mistakes that could undermine decades of state-building efforts. The intellectuals of 1990 attempted to warn the nation of the dangers it faced. Today, more than fourteen years after the establishment of the non-transitional Federal Government in 2012, a critical question must be asked: Who will assume the responsibility of bringing national voices together, reducing political tensions, and safeguarding the future of Somali statehood? The time has come for Somali intellectuals to move beyond isolated statements, media commentary, and political alignments toward meaningful consultations and a collective effort to identify national solutions. History remembers more than the leaders who held political power. It also remembers those who demonstrated the courage to defend the public interest, those who worked to prevent national tragedies, and those who remained silent when their country needed them most. Somali statehood is a national inheritance achieved through decades of struggle and immense sacrifice. It is not the property of any particular government, political party, or group in power. It is a collective responsibility belonging to the entire Somali people. The question, therefore, remains: Where are the Somali intellectuals and respected national figures who will stand up today to safeguard Somalia's future? Somalia must not wait for another national catastrophe to recognize the value of statehood. What the country needs is an awakened national conscience, leadership willing to accept constructive advice, and intellectuals with the courage to speak the truth. A nation must be saved while there is still an opportunity to correct its course—not after its collapse has become an irreversible reality. Writer: Amb. After 20 years of a lot of blood and sacrifice we are handing over security to our Somali brothers,” Gen. Muhoozi Kainerugaba, chief of Uganda’s defense forces, wrote on X. advertisements Ugandan authorities have not publicly announced how many troops are leaving, which bases will be handed over first or when the withdrawal will be completed. Uganda remains the largest troop contributor to the African Union Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia, or AUSSOM. The African Union authorized 4,500 Ugandan troops for the mission, which replaced the African Union Transition Mission in Somalia at the start of 2025. AUSSOM’s mandate includes supporting Somali forces against al-Shabab, protecting civilians and key infrastructure, and gradually transferring security responsibilities to Somali security institutions. The mission’s current transition plan envisages a phased drawdown toward a final exit by December 2029, subject to security conditions. Uganda first deployed troops to Somalia in March 2007 as the lead contingent in the African Union Mission in Somalia, or AMISOM, becoming one of the longest-serving foreign military contributors to the country’s security operations. Ugandan forces have since fought in some of the most significant battles against al-Shabab and have operated across Mogadishu and large parts of Lower Shabelle. The deployment has also come at a heavy cost. Ugandan troops have suffered repeated casualties in al-Shabab attacks, including major assaults on African Union bases over the course of the mission. The announcement comes as AUSSOM faces persistent funding shortages. The African Union Peace and Security Council has repeatedly warned that inadequate and unpredictable financing threatens the mission’s operations and has called for additional international support. The AU has also emphasized that decisions over AUSSOM’s future and troop withdrawals should be based on assessments of conditions on the ground and coordinated with Somalia to avoid creating security gaps. Uganda has remained a central part of that security architecture. Earlier this year, the African Union praised Kampala for deploying additional troops to Somalia on a bilateral basis as a temporary response to deteriorating security conditions. Al-Shabab, an al-Qaeda-linked militant group, continues to control or operate across parts of rural southern and central Somalia despite nearly two decades of military pressure from Somali forces and their international partners. Kainerugaba’s announcement therefore represents a significant shift in Uganda’s long-running role in Somalia, but it remains unclear whether the move marks the beginning of a full national withdrawal or a phased reduction coordinated with AUSSOM and Somali authorities. The decision was announced in an official notice published in the US Federal Register on October 27, 2026, following an assessment of Somalia's port security procedures. The Coast Guard said Somalia was not currently maintaining effective anti-terrorism measures at its ports, prompting Washington to impose special security requirements on ships departing from the country and heading to US ports. The measures are intended to strengthen maritime security and prevent potential terrorist threats from reaching American ports. The decision was made under powers granted by the Maritime Transportation Security Act and other legislation governing port security and maritime safety. Somalia is among 24 countries identified by the US Coast Guard as failing to maintain effective anti-terrorism security measures at their ports. The list also includes Iran, Iraq, Libya, Sudan, Syria, Yemen, Venezuela and North Korea, among other countries. The notice states that the decision took effect on October 27, the day it was published. It was signed by Admiral Nathan A. Moore, the Coast Guard's Deputy Commandant for Operations. The additional requirements mean vessels arriving in the United States from Somali ports will be subject to enhanced security procedures. However, the notice does not detail all the specific measures that affected ships will be required to follow. The designation could have implications for maritime operators using Somali ports, potentially increasing security checks and compliance requirements for vessels bound for the United States. Somalia has been working to strengthen its maritime institutions and port security as part of broader efforts to improve trade, protect its coastline and attract international investment. The Coast Guard's assessment, however, indicates that Washington considers existing anti-terrorism safeguards at Somali ports insufficient under its maritime security standards. The Maritime Security Centre–Indian Ocean (MSCIO), which supports the EU's Operation ATALANTA, said the Iranian fishing vessel Azini was reportedly hijacked at approximately 09:00 UTC on October 29. In an update displayed on October 31, MSCIO said the vessel was approaching a maritime traffic lane and could potentially be used as a mothership to support additional piracy operations. The warning does not establish that the Azini has been used to launch attacks. The safety of its crew remains unknown, and authorities have not identified those responsible for the reported hijacking. The vessel's reported movement toward a shipping traffic lane has raised concerns about possible threats to merchant ships operating off Somalia's northeastern coast. A fishing vessel used as a pirate mothership could serve as a base for attacks beyond the immediate location of the original incident, potentially exposing other vessels to additional security risks. MSCIO has not reported any confirmed attacks launched from the Azini. Shipping Operators Urged to Remain Vigilant MSCIO urged vessels operating near the reported incident to maintain heightened vigilance, follow maritime security guidance and report suspicious activity. The advisory comes as Operation ATALANTA investigates the circumstances surrounding the reported seizure. For commercial shipping operators, the immediate concern is whether the incident remains isolated or develops into a wider threat along nearby maritime routes. The potential use of the Azini as a mothership is central to the warning, although authorities have not established that the vessel is being used for piracy operations. No confirmed follow-on attacks have been identified in MSCIO's notice. advertisements Incident Reported Off Puntland Coast Puntland Post, a regional news outlet, separately reported that the incident occurred off Banderbayla on Somalia's northeastern coast. The publication also reported that two Somali guards were among those aboard the Iranian vessel. Neither detail has been independently verified, and Puntland Post did not identify the sources behind its account. MSCIO has not provided a verified account from the crew or established who carried out the reported hijacking. The available information leaves the vessel's current status, the condition of those aboard and the identity of the suspected attackers unresolved. Investigation Focuses on Potential Piracy Threat Operation ATALANTA is investigating the reported incident as maritime authorities continue to warn nearby vessels of a possible security threat. The MSCIO advisory does not establish the circumstances of the initial boarding or confirm whether the vessel is currently under the control of suspected pirates. For commercial ship operators, the next critical development will be whether authorities can establish the Azini's status and determine if the vessel poses an active threat to nearby shipping. Until then, MSCIO's guidance remains focused on heightened vigilance and reporting suspicious activity, with the risk of further pirate attacks still unconfirmed.
